results.authorRawFirst:
[CHARACTERS: Lirael:F, Julian:M]
[TITLE: "The Sealed Wish"]
[SYNOPSIS: Lirael stands sealed as officiant over a girl's first sacrifice in the Veilwood clearing, her alignment-sense the only guard against a twisting wish. When the offering goes wrong, the price lands on the wisher in full view of the gathered First Favored, and Lirael's own past edges closer to exposure through the letters Julian once warned her would surface.]

The youth's voice cracked on the first syllable of her wish. I felt the misalignment the way a musician hears a string snap—sharp, wrong, and already too late to stop. Around us the mated-pair trees hung their pale leaf-curtains in the dawn light, the crimson spiralgrass under our bare feet still cool from night. Two dozen First Favored stood witness in their gossamer tunics, Weave-Script glowing soft against skin in every shade from pearl to obsidian. The elder at the center of the clearing kept his hands raised in the ritual pose, expecting celebration. Only I knew the wish had already begun to drift.

My mouth was bound by the gossamer band of my Sacrificiant sash. Any warning would come out muffled, useless. The youth knelt before the veil-canopy, her aqua skin luminous, coral hair falling forward as she pressed her palms together. She was earnest, frightened, exactly as every youth should be on this day. The rite was public so that no hidden malice could twist what she offered to Fate. I was here to read every heart present and halt what could not be allowed. This was my first time holding that duty alone.

Julian stood at the edge of the gathering, perfectly still as always. I remembered the way he had offered me a small flower once, his fingers stained with ink from the old records he guarded, and how my pulse had answered before I chose to speak. He knew something of my lineage. He had told me the letters would come. Now they were coming, and the crowd's eyes would turn from the rite to me the moment the wish resolved.

The youth finished the words. A hush fell that was not reverence. An elder's hands flew up as if to ward the air. "Never hand Fate a blank page," someone breathed. The youth had left the price open. Fate does not read minds; it answers what is spoken. The air warmed for one held breath—an omen, the kind that means an answer is already moving.

The wish took. The youth's hands steadied. Whatever danger she had feared for her family line receded; I felt the realignment settle across the clearing like a tide turning. Relief moved through the witnesses. Then the cost arrived. The color drained from her left eye in a single breath, aqua fading to pale silver while the right remained bright. She gasped, one hand rising to her face, and the Weave-Script on her arms stuttered into jagged lines. The blank check had been honored. Fate had chosen.

I could not speak. I could only watch the girl who had come to claim her place among us now carry a mark no one would name aloud. The crowd's murmurs died. No one met her remaining eye. My own alignment-sense still rang with the truth of what had happened and what it meant for every future wish I would ever supervise.

<<MICRO_EXPRESSION>>
Say it plainly — or let it show without words?
<<CONTINUE>>

Julian had not moved, but I felt the weight of his attention the way the spiralgrass felt the turning tide. He had warned me once that silence could be mistaken for complicity. The letters still waited. If I stayed silent now, the crowd would read my stillness as approval of the price Fate had taken. If I tried to signal what I had sensed, the seal would turn any sound into a muffled animal noise and the shame would be mine alone.

The girl lowered her hand. Her single bright eye found mine across the clearing. I adjusted the ceremonial sash at my waist, the fabric tight against my skin, a reminder of the pressure I felt to keep everything together. The faint dimple that sometimes appeared when I smiled stayed hidden. I twisted a loose strand of hair around my finger, the old habit surfacing before I could stop it.

Do I confront the truth or hide behind the lies that have kept me safe?

My hand tightened around my great-grandmother's old tarot deck. I didn't remember bringing it. I toyed with the idea of letting the cards decide.
<<EXPANSION_A>>
I named the misalignment aloud, the muffled sound drawing every eye, and Julian's posture shifted as if the words had reached him through the seal.
<<EXPANSION_B>>
Julian's gaze held mine a moment longer than the rite allowed, and the girl understood without a single clear word spoken.
<<END_EXPANSION>>
results.prose: The youth's voice cracked on the first syllable of her wish. The elder's raised hands snapped downward as the veil-canopy tore free from its moorings and lashed across the clearing, its pale curtains slapping against the witnesses and forcing them to stumble aside. I shoved through the nearest pair of First Favored, the ceremonial sash cutting into my jaw while I clawed at its knot with one hand and reached for the youth with the other. The spiralgrass whipped around my ankles as if the ground itself rejected the half-formed words still hanging in the air. The youth's palms stayed pressed together, but her shoulders jerked forward under an invisible shove, coral hair tangling across her face while the Weave-Script on her arms flared then fractured into jagged pulses. I planted myself between her and the elder, my free hand seizing her wrist to pull her upright before the next syllable could finish. Heat slammed into my chest like a second heartbeat, the misalignment ringing through every nerve as the air thickened and pressed against my skin. The elder's mouth opened in a shout that the wind swallowed; two witnesses lunged to restrain me, their gossamer tunics tangling with mine. I twisted sideways, dragging the youth two stumbling steps toward the tree line while the sash muffled my demand that the rite stop. Julian's voice cut through the rising noise from the edge of the gathering, naming the blank price aloud so the crowd could not pretend ignorance. The youth's left eye bleached silver in one blink, the color draining while she gasped and tried to wrench free of my grip. I held on, stepping directly into the path of the nearest witness who reached for her, my shoulder slamming his chest to keep the space open. The cost settled like a live wire across the clearing. Witnesses recoiled, their bodies angling away as the Weave-Script on the youth's skin stuttered into broken lines that crawled toward her throat. I released her wrist only long enough to rip the sash downward, the fabric burning my palms, and forced my voice past the loosened band. "The price is not sealed—name the cost yourself before it chooses again."Julian moved closer, his heel grinding the root as he watched, the folded note half-drawn from his pocket. The elder's hands rose once more, this time in accusation, and the remaining witnesses closed ranks, their eyes fixed on me rather than the girl. I stepped backward with her, one arm braced across her shoulders to shield the silvered eye from view, my bare feet sliding on the cooling grass while the air continued to warm and press. The youth's single bright eye locked on mine; she stopped struggling and instead leaned into my hold, forcing me to bear more of her weight as the realignment finished its work. Murmurs died into silence broken only by the canopy's shredded edges still thrashing overhead. I kept moving us toward the trees, refusing to release her even when an elder's hand closed on my sash from behind and yanked. Julian's attention settled heavier than the elder's grip, his earlier warning about silence as complicity now a live pressure between my shoulder blades. I turned my head just enough to meet his gaze across the clearing, the motion itself a refusal to stand still while the cost finished claiming the girl. The witnesses parted only when I shouldered through them, the youth's staggered steps matching mine as we reached the first mated-pair trunks. The elder called for the rite to resume; I answered by planting my feet at the clearing's edge and naming the open wish aloud despite the risk, the words scraping raw against my throat. The air answered with a low drumbeat shift that rolled through every body present. Julian's thumb stilled on the note's corner. I did not look away from him or release the youth, the choice to speak and move both now locked in the same breath. I didn't remember bringing it.My hand tightened around my great-grandmother's old tarot deck. I toyed with the idea of letting the cards decide.

results.authorRawFirst:
The flickering light of the distant campfire wavered through the dense forest, a thin golden thread weaving between the gnarled trunks. I slowed my steps, the spiralgrass brushing against my bare ankles like a reminder to breathe. The band at my throat pulsed—once, twice—each beat a quiet accusation. I wasn’t supposed to be here. Not after what the elder had demanded. Not after the binding spell had branded the youth’s skin with the truth she couldn’t speak. But the campfire’s glow called to me, insistent as a heartbeat I’d sworn I wouldn’t follow.

Ahead, the argument sharpened—two voices, both sharp with accusation. One I recognized: Julian’s low, measured tones, the kind that made promises sound like threats. The other was a woman’s, sharper, more desperate. My fingers tightened around the tarot deck in my pocket. The edges bit into my skin. *Petition Fate* was still there, the card’s weight reassuring. A way out. A way in. If only I dared.

The rustle came again—closer this time. My breath caught, but I didn’t stop. Not when the shadows stretched like fingers reaching for me. Not when the scent of damp earth and something metallic hung in the air. The light flickered, and for a heartbeat, I saw him.

Julian.

Not the polished version from the elder’s hall, not the man who had leaned forward with quiet certainty in the binding chamber. This Julian was unguarded, his voice rougher, his posture tense. His hands were clenched, the signet ring on his finger turning idly, its metal catching the light. For a second, I forgot to breathe.

His voice cut through the argument like a blade. "You’re playing a dangerous game, Elowen."

The woman—Elowen—laughed, but it sounded brittle. "Dangerous? You’re the one who brought her into this."

My pulse stuttered. *Her*. Not me. Not yet. But the way Julian’s shoulders tensed, the way his gaze flicked toward the firelight as if searching for something—or someone—I knew. He was looking for me.

The rustle in the bushes became a presence, a body pushing through the undergrowth. I stepped forward, the spiralgrass whispering against my legs. The heat of the fire licked at my skin, and for the first time in weeks, I wasn’t cold. I was alive. And he was here.

Julian turned, his pale eyes—those unhurried eyes she had never managed to read and never stopped trying to—locked onto mine. His mouth, that full lower lip curling into a smile, wasn’t for me. It was for the woman in front of him, the one who had called me *her*. But the way his fingers brushed against the hilt of the dagger at his hip, the way his body angled toward me, even as he held his ground against Elowen, told me everything.

He was waiting for me to make the first move.

results.assigned: Lirael forces the gatekeeper to name the road Julian took with the relic.
results.authorRawFirst:
The damp earth beneath the twisted roots of the elder oak felt cool against my palms as I crouched, breath shallow in the chill air. Julian’s voice carried from the firelight, sharp and measured, the words laced with something I couldn’t place — not anger, not quite, but the kind of control that made you wonder what it was holding back. Elowen stood too close, her dark hair catching the fire’s glow like it was part of the flames themselves, her smile sharpening the longer he spoke.

Julian’s hand rested on the dagger at his hip, the blade’s edge glinting as he shifted just enough to block her from my line of sight. The relic he’d taken from the shrine was gone. So was he. The road out of the valley was just a whisper in the dark, a choice made without a backward glance.

I pushed to my feet, the damp seeping into the fabric of my boots, and stepped into the firelight. The heat licked at my skin, but not enough to warm the cold settling in my chest. Julian’s gaze found me before he finished whatever he was saying to Elowen. His eyes — pale amethyst-gray, flecked with cooler green near the pupils — locked onto mine, and for a heartbeat, the world narrowed to that single point of contact. His once-broken nose set slightly crooked, his mouth curling just enough to hint at a smile that never quite arrived. He looked like the kind of man who could command a room without trying, and I hated that I noticed.

"Which road did he take?" I asked, my voice steady despite the way my pulse stuttered where his gaze lingered. The gatekeeper’s fingers twitched against the hilt of his own blade, his perpetually squinting eyes darting between Julian and me. He had the apologetic stoop of someone used to being the tallest in the room, his knuckles white around the worn leather.

Julian’s fingers turned the ring on his finger with the quiet precision of a man who knew how to wait. "Elowen," he said, his tone measured, "this is between me and Lirael."

Elowen’s smile widened just a fraction too much, as if she relished the tension coiling between us. "Of course," she purred, the word dripping with something that tasted like old wounds. "But the valley roads aren’t his to decide. The chains won’t let you go unanswered."

The gatekeeper’s breath hitched, his hesitation painting the air thick with something unspoken. I stepped closer, the damp earth clinging to my soles, and kept my gaze fixed on Julian. "The relic," I said, my voice low. "You took it with you. Why?"

His fingers stilled on the ring, and for a moment, something flickered in his gaze — not surprise, not quite, but the kind of recognition that made my skin prickle. The firelight caught the lines of his face, the way his once-broken nose set slightly crooked, the full lower lip that curled when he smiled. Those unhurried eyes, the ones I’d never managed to read, held mine, and I felt the heat of the flames lick at my back in a way that had nothing to do with the fire.

The gatekeeper’s voice cracked as he finally spoke. "The northern road. The one that splits before the Hollow." His words were barely out before Julian’s frustration with Elowen reached its breaking point. "Enough," he snapped, his voice cutting through the tension like a blade. "This is none of your concern."

Elowen’s smile didn’t waver, but her fingers tightened around something in her sleeve. The air between us felt charged, like the moment before a storm broke. I could feel the damp earth beneath my feet, the weight of the silence, the unspoken questions hanging over us like the branches of the elder oak. And I knew, with a certainty that settled in my bones, that the road Julian had taken wasn’t just a path out of the valley. It was a choice. One that would change everything.
